title: Vending Machine Simulator
story: You're staring at the office vending machine, deciding between candy and chips. Behind that glass panel, a computer is running functions: one maps button numbers to items, another checks if you inserted enough money. You're going to rebuild that logic.
why: A vending machine simulator combines if/elif item selection with Boolean affordability checks — two functions that model a real embedded system's decision logic.
analogy: The vending machine is like a restaurant with a menu and a cashier. `vend()` is the menu — it translates numbers to items. `get_price()` is the price tag on each item. `can_afford()` is the cashier checking your wallet against the price. The cashier doesn't need to memorize prices — they just look at the price tag (`get_price`). Change the price tag, and the cashier automatically knows the new price.
try_it: Add three more items to the vending machine (slots 5, 6, 7) with their own names and prices. Then write a `buy_item(money: Int, item: Int) -> Str` function that returns the item name if affordable or 'Insufficient funds' if not.
tips: get_price returns 0 for unknown items — can_afford checks for this edge case
can_afford calls get_price instead of duplicating the price data
Use `>=` to check affordability — having exactly the right amount is enough
The else clause in vend handles invalid item numbers gracefully
common_mistakes: Hardcoding prices directly in can_afford instead of calling get_price — duplicated data
Using `>` instead of `>=` — someone with exactly 100 cents can't buy a 100-cent item
Forgetting the else clause in vend — unknown item numbers should return something meaningful
Not checking for price == 0 in can_afford — unknown items should not be affordable
